text.title: Demo Recap Email Template Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules with rationale + source for demo-recap-email-template. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Every recap email MUST carry six blocks in this order: header (sprint + date + attendees), demoed features (linked to tickets), decisions made (with named decider), scope deltas (added / removed / parked), open items (with named owner + due date), next demo date + scope.
rule.rationale: A fixed block order makes an omission visible: a reader who scans for scope deltas and finds no such block knows the section is missing, rather than assuming nothing changed. Free-form recaps drop exactly the uncomfortable sections, deltas and open items, because the author writes from the memory of a demo that went well instead of from a template that asks.

rule.statement: Every decision MUST name the human who made it; ambiguous attribution ('the team agreed') is forbidden — use HiPPO-override discipline from facilitation-anti-patterns.
rule.rationale: The team agreed leaves nobody to ask when the decision is later disputed, and nobody who feels the weight of it when it is made. Naming the decider gives the reader a specific person to challenge inside the objection window, and it forecloses the standard outsource pattern where the vendor believes the client decided and the client believes the vendor did.

rule.statement: Each scope delta MUST cite the ticket id (or new ticket created) where the change is captured; prose-only scope deltas are forbidden.
rule.rationale: A scope change described only in an email lives in a thread nobody re-reads at invoicing time. Bound to a ticket id, the change travels into the backlog, the estimate and the invoice as one object. Prose-only deltas are how a fixed-bid engagement discovers at the end that it built work nobody priced.

rule.statement: Each open item MUST have a single named owner and an ISO date; a bare to-be-decided placeholder is rejected — escalate to sponsor instead.
rule.rationale: A to-be-decided placeholder is a shared owner, which is no owner: each party assumes the other is chasing it, and the item resurfaces unchanged at the next demo. If the owner genuinely cannot be named, what is missing is authority rather than information, and that is a sponsor decision. Carrying the placeholder just delays it by a sprint.

rule.statement: Recap email MUST be sent within 24 hours of demo end; later than that the client memory drift dominates and the email loses authority.
rule.rationale: The recap is authoritative only while both sides still hold the same memory of the room. After a day the client has reconstructed the demo around what they expected to see, so the email stops being a record and becomes a claim, which invites negotiation over what was said instead of confirmation of it.

rule.statement: Email asks client for ack or objection within 48 hours of send; silence beyond that window is recorded as 'tacit acceptance' in the engagement log.
rule.rationale: Silence is otherwise unusable, because it means both agreed and not read yet. Declaring the window in advance turns silence into something the client chose, and gives the vendor a defensible reading of it later. Without the declared window, an unanswered email is evidence of nothing at all.

rule.statement: If the engagement has no recurring demo cadence or the client refuses written records, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: The template's value is a repeated written record that accumulates into an audit trail across sprints. With no cadence there is nothing to accumulate, and a client who refuses written records reads each recap as case-building against them, which makes the artefact a relationship cost rather than a protection.
